title_en: Homily on “In the Beginning Was the Word”
author: Basil of Caesarea
addressee: a Christian congregation hearing the Gospel read
occasion: Basil preaches on the opening of John’s Gospel, which has just been read, to arm his hearers against arguments that the Son is a creature who once did not exist.
argument: Basil urges his hearers not to admire John’s opening words from a distance but to grasp their power. He shows that “in the beginning” excludes any time before the Word, and that “was” refutes those who say the Son once was not. He explains why John says “Word” rather than “Son”: the term teaches that the Son comes forth from the Father without passion, as a mind’s word expresses the whole mind. He then expounds “and the Word was with God” as preserving the distinct reality of Father and Son, and “the Word was God” as confessing the Word’s full divinity. He closes by giving the congregation the four phrases, with the fourth being the repeated “was,” as a fixed defense and foundation for faith.

outline.move: Basil praises John as the greatest of the Gospel voices and warns that the opening words demand more than admiration.
He distinguishes the unique beginning of all things from ordinary beginnings and insists that “in the beginning was” leaves no room for a time when the Word was not.
He rules out human and angelic speech as the meaning of “Word” and explains why “Word” reveals the Son’s passionless generation from the Father.
He expounds “the Word was with God” and “the Word was God,” then gives the four phrases as an unshakable defense against blasphemy.

key_terms.sense: The unique beginning of all things, beyond which nothing can be thought; not an ordinary starting point.
The Son of God, so named to show his passionless generation from the Father as the perfect expression of the Father’s mind.
The “was” of John 1:1, indicating the Word’s eternal existence without beginning.
The only-begotten Son of God, the one whose glory the opponents attack.
The impious claim that the Son is a creature who once did not exist, or that Father and Son are one underlying thing.
The distinct reality or subsistence of Father and Son, which “with God” is meant to preserve.
The Son’s being begotten from the Father, which Basil insists is without passion or time.
Without passion or suffering, used of the Son’s generation from the Father.
Worldly wisdom, the learning of those outside the truth who admired John’s words.
Those outside the truth of the faith, non-Christian thinkers.

scripture: Basil quotes the Septuagint and the Greek New Testament. He cites Proverbs and 1 Corinthians. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint where relevant; modern citations should use standard English Bible names and numbering, noting LXX differences when they occur.
uncertain: The precise date and occasion of delivery are not stated in the text.
The identity of the opponents Basil quotes is not named; they are characterized only by their arguments.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He closes by giving the congregation the four phrases, with the fourth being the repeated "was,"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν. Τέταρτον εἰπὲ τὸ, Ἦν, καὶ καταργήσεις αὐτῶν τὸ, Οὐκ ἦν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The four phrases are: (1) "In the beginning was the Word," (2) "and the Word was with God," (3) "and the Word was God," (4) "This one was in the beginning with God" (Οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν). The fourth is not a repeated "was" but a distinct clause. Basil then adds a fifth instruction: "Say a fourth time the 'was'" (Τέταρτον εἰπὲ τὸ, Ἦν) as a rhetorical flourish to emphasize the refutation of "was not."

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Holy Spirit through the Gospel ... sections: ["1"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἵνα τοίνυν μηδενὶ λέγειν ἐξῇ τὰ τοιαῦτα, προλαβὸν τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον διὰ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, Ἐν ἀρχῇ, φησίν, ἦν ὁ Λόγος.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Holy Spirit speaks through the Gospel in section 1, but also in section 4 where Basil writes "Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος" and attributes the teaching to the Spirit's instruction ("ὑποτάγηθι τῷ Κυρίῳ" following the Spirit's declaration). More importantly, the brief misses that the Holy Spirit is also the one who "foreknew" (προῄδει) the objections in section 1.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ γὰρ ᾐνίξατο ἡμῖν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, ὡς καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων ἰδίαν ἐχόντων γλῶσσαν, εἰπών· Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώ πων λαλῶ καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Apostle is cited in section 2, not section 3. The reference appears at the end of section 2: "Καὶ γὰρ ᾐνίξατο ἡμῖν ὁ Ἀπόστολος..." This is before the section break; section 3 begins with "Ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ λόγου διπλῆ τίς ἐστιν ἔννοια."

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Apostle ... who: "Cited allusively (ᾐνίξατο) for the idea that angels have their own tongues; Basil does not name him as Paul."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ᾐνίξατο ἡμῖν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, ὡς καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων ἰδίαν ἐχόντων γλῶσσαν, εἰπών· Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων λαλῶ καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Apostle is named as "ὁ Ἀπόστολος" (the Apostle), not left unnamed. While Basil does not explicitly say "Paul," the title "the Apostle" without further specification in Greek patristic literature typically refers to Paul. The citation is not particularly allusive—it directly quotes 1 Corinthians 13:1 with clear attribution.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He explains why John says "Word" rather than "Son": the term teaches that the Son comes forth from the Father without passion, as a mind's word expresses the whole mind.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἰ δὲ εἶπεν· Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Υἱὸς, τῇ προσηγορίᾳ τοῦ Υἱοῦ συνεισῆλθεν ἄν σοι ἡ περὶ τοῦ πάθους ἔννοια. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ παρ' ἡμῖν τὰ γεννῶντα χρόνῳ γεννᾷ, καὶ ἐμπαθῶς γεννᾷ, διὰ τοῦτο προλαβὼν, Λόγον εἶπε, προδιορθούμενος τὰς ἀπρεπεῖς ὑπολήψεις
_unresolved_facts.fix: Basil gives two reasons for "Word" rather than "Son": (1) to avoid the connotation of passion/suffering (πάθος) associated with human sonship, and (2) to avoid the ideas of temporal generation and passionate generation (χρόνῳ γεννᾷ, καὶ ἐμπαθῶς γεννᾷ). The brief omits the temporal aspect and overemphasizes the cognitive/mind analogy at the expense of the apologetic against anthropomorphic conceptions of divine generation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ["2"], move: "He distinguishes the unique beginning of all things from ordinary beginnings and insists that 'in the beginning was' leaves no room for a time when the Word was not."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὸ γὰρ, Πρὸ τοῦ, χρονική ἐστι φωνή... Τὸν δὲ τοῦ χρόνου ποιητὴν πῶς εὔλογον ταῖς χρονικαῖς προσηγορίαις ὑποκειμένην ἔχειν τὴν γέννησιν;
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 2 also contains the crucial argument that "before" (πρὸ τοῦ) is a temporal expression that cannot apply to the Creator of time. The outline move understates the sophistication of Basil's argument: he not only insists on "was" but demonstrates the category error of applying temporal language to the timeless.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The devil ... who: "The thief who steals Christian teaching for his own spokesmen."
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κλέπτης γὰρ ὁ διάβολος, καὶ τὰ ἡμέτερα ἐκφερομυθῶν πρὸς τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ ὑποφήτας.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The devil is described as a thief who "carries our things out in myths/stories to his own spokesmen" (ἐκφερομυθῶν). The term ὑποφήτας means "prophets" or "mouthpieces," not merely "spokesmen" in a neutral sense—the connotation is of false prophets who receive stolen Christian teaching.
